title: The Cargo Is Still Out There
logline: A low rock above a bay on a dry southern coast, where two lines cut into the stone are the only written evidence that a harbour ever stood under it, and where the one cargo anybody can still point to lies four kilometres out and thirty-three metres down and is never, at any point, shown.
human_question: If the only thing that survived of everything people wanted here is the receipt, what would a receipt say about what I want?

place.what_kind_of_place: A low granite rock standing at the edge of the ocean on a hot, dry, thinly built stretch of southern coast, with a small fishing hamlet at its foot, a wide pale beach that is a protected turtle nesting ground, and the mouth of a slow, silt-brown river four kilometres to the west where it pushes out through a shifting sand bar. On top of the rock is a working temple with a whitewashed stupa at the highest point, rebuilt in the twentieth century over much older footings; on the face of the rock itself are two lines of early letters. Around the base, in and out of the sand, lie the excavated remains of an ancient harbour: the pillar stumps of a landing jetty, brick and stone footings identified as a customs office, and an abandoned quarry where one big half-dressed pillar, covered in drill marks, still lies on its side within sight of the water. Nothing about the place announces itself. A visitor who did not know would see a rock, a temple, a beach and some stones.
place.why_it_is_worth_watching: Four things carry the film with the sound off, and three of them are about light rather than event. First, the inscription: two lines of shallow letters that are invisible for most of the day and, for perhaps twenty minutes when the sun is low enough, come up out of the rock face as hard black shadow and then go again. Second, the mouth of the river: brown water meeting green water in a curved line across a sand bar, with surf breaking on both sides of the join and nothing else in the frame. Third, the half-cut pillar lying in the grass and sand, a worked object abandoned mid-job, filmed close enough for the drill marks to read as tool marks and not as texture. And fourth, the film's actual payoff, which is a refusal: one enormous locked-off frame of flat open water, held far past the point of comfort, with nothing happening on it at all.
place.what_moves_or_changes: Almost nothing built moves, and the camera mostly does not either. What changes is the sun on the rock face, which gives the letters and then takes them back; the bar at the river mouth, which shifts with the swell; the tide over the jetty stumps; and the boats, which go out and come back on their own business. Weather comes in off the water and the horizon goes from hard to soft. In season, turtles come ashore at night, which the film knows about and does not film. The one thing in the piece that never changes is the surface of the water over the wreck, which is the point.
place.when_it_looks_best: The inscription only in raking light, within the first or the last hour of sun, and only on a clear morning or evening; outside that window it does not exist on camera. The river mouth at first light, before the wind gets up and flattens the colour join. The held water shot deliberately at the least flattering hour of the day, flat high sun, no golden light, no drama on the horizon, because the shot is about there being nothing to see. The drier, calmer months on this coast rather than the wet north-east monsoon stretch, when the sea here is rough and brown and the sand bar is unreadable.

two_layers.without_the_philosophy: A quiet, hot, extremely still coastal film that keeps promising something offshore and never delivers it. It opens on letters coming up out of a rock in low light, works down to the emptied apparatus at the rock's foot, crosses to a river mouth, and then stops dead on a single held frame of open water while a voice says precisely what is lying under it and how far away. Nothing is revealed. The letters come back at last light and go out again. Someone who never hears a word of the philosophy still gets a complete piece with a build, a held centre and an ending that lands as a withholding rather than a reveal, and which is all the stronger for having been announced in advance.
two_layers.with_the_philosophy: The same footage becomes an argument about what evidence can and cannot carry. The voice sets the ancient books' eight-way sorting of wanting beside the only sorting this place actually performed: a duty assessed on goods and stamped in clay with a lion to certify that it had been paid. The stamp is real, dateable and legible. It certifies a payment and nothing else. Beside it the film puts the sources' own three switches — glad or flat, with a justifying story or without, rising of itself or needing a push — not one of which leaves any mark in clay, on stone, or on a camera sensor. And then it withholds the object. The film about wanting refuses to show the one thing anybody in it wanted, and by refusing, says the thing a camera can never say.

sequence.on_screen: First light, long lens, locked off on a patch of rock face maybe a metre across. Two lines of shallow early letters sitting in raking shadow. The frame is held long enough that the shadows visibly shorten and the letters start to go.
sequence.voice: Two lines, cut into the face of this rock. In translation: success — the customs duty of the harbour here, King Gamani Abhaya granted to the monastery. That is the whole of it. And that sentence is the only written evidence anybody has ever found that there was a harbour under this rock at all. No plan of it, no ledger, no manifest, no list of goods. What survived is a receipt.

sequence.on_screen: Down at the base. Low tide over a line of squared stone pillar stumps running out into the water. Then, in one slow pan on the ground, brick and stone footings in dry earth, and beyond them a large half-dressed pillar lying on its side in the sand and scrub, its whole length covered in unfinished drill marks.
sequence.voice: An old Sinhala compendium of the Abhidhamma sets out the ordinary occasions on which a greed-rooted mind arises, and a working harbour is most of that list without a word needing to be added. Doing many things in order to get wealth. Getting it. Guarding what has been got. Paying it out to obtain the things you want. Preparing those things, and using them [C005-M:L5]. And then the flat remark that follows: that for a person living apart from the teaching, most minds from waking until sleep are of this kind [C005-M:L7].

sequence.on_screen: Static, wide, unglamorous: the footings of one building in flat early light, a rectangle of low courses in the dust with nothing standing on them. Nothing is held up to camera and nothing is handled. Just the ground where it was.
sequence.voice: Under the sand here they found the footings of a building identified as the customs office, with an elephant putting its trunk into lotus flowers cut into its ornament, and clay seals stamped with a lion. The seal was the proof that duty on the goods and on the cargo had been paid. Wanting was assessed, priced, sealed and handed to monks. And the same book, in the same breath as its list, says that the same getting and guarding and spending, done out of faith or kindness, or out of plain practical sense about what is actually useful, is not counted against anybody at all [C005-M:L9]. Which means that the lion certified the payment. It certified nothing else.

sequence.on_screen: The same patch of rock face as the opening, now at midday. Flat grey stone. The letters are not there. The frame is identical and the writing has simply gone.
sequence.voice: The companion chapter sorts this one wanting eight ways, and it does it on three switches. Feeling: it can come glad, when what turns up is pleasant, or completely flat, when what turns up is neither pleasant nor unpleasant [C006-P:L25] [C006-P:L74]. A story: it can arrive with a justification, the kind that says there are no consequences, or that he had plenty anyway, or it can arrive with none [C006-P:L33]. And a push: some of it rises sharply, of its own nature, needing no urging whatever [C006-P:L44], and some of it needs urging, which can be somebody else's, or can be a person taking their own hanging-back mind and talking it forward [C006-M:L5]. Two by two by two. Eight. The book then ranks them for strength, and two of its rankings are not what anyone would guess: it puts the flat one above the glad one, and the one with a story above the one without [C006-M:L19].

sequence.on_screen: The river mouth, from the beach, very long lens, camera static. Brown water and green water meeting in a curve over the bar, surf on both sides of the line. A boat crosses the frame from left to right over about ninety seconds and leaves it empty again.
sequence.voice: And when it lists what makes the sharp, unprompted kind likelier, it does not talk about anybody's character. It talks about a sound mind and a sound body, about patience, about being practised at the thing you are doing, and about getting the right weather and the right food [C006-P:L46–L52]. Conditions, not verdicts. It also describes, without any contempt at all, the person who fully believes that actions have consequences and cannot hold the wanting back anyway, mostly out of long habit [C006-P:L66]. Not one item on either list leaves a mark. There is no clay you could press any of that into.

sequence.on_screen: The held shot. From the top of the rock, long lens, locked off, flat high sun: open water and an empty horizon, no boat, no bird, no island, nothing. The frame does not move and is not cut away from. It runs for minutes.
sequence.voice: About four kilometres out from where you are looking, and thirty-three metres down, there is a ship. It has been there for something like two thousand years, and it is the oldest wreck anybody has found in this ocean. On it: a mound of corroded metal bars fused together into one lump, several hundred glass ingots, grinding stones, pottery. Every item of that was carried here because somebody, at the other end, wanted it. Nobody who wanted it ever received it. The site is under excavation, and we are not going to show it to you. The one object this entire film is about is under that water, four kilometres that way, and it stays there.

sequence.on_screen: Last light. The same metre of rock face as beat one and beat four. The letters come back out of the stone as the sun drops, hold for a couple of minutes, and go flat again as it sets. Final frame: the water, dark, empty, in the last of the light.
sequence.voice: A camera cannot show greed. It never could, and neither could the clay: the seal recorded that a sum had been paid, not what anybody was thinking when they paid it. Two thousand years on, this is what is left of the entire arrangement. A stone with an amount on it. And a cargo nobody received. The sentence names the harbour, the king and the monastery, and it says nothing whatever about why any of it was wanted.

concept_merge.why_together: Read fresh, the two digests are the two halves of one machine, and this place is where the machine's output and its mechanism can be put side by side and shown to be different kinds of thing. C005 supplies the occasions and the rule. Its list of occasions is not a charge sheet; it is a description of ordinary life, and the part of it that matters here is the wealth sequence — doing many things to get wealth, getting it, guarding what has been got, paying it out to obtain what is wanted, preparing those things and using them [C005-M:L5] — followed by the flat statement that for someone living apart from the teaching most minds from waking to sleep run this way [C005-M:L7]. Then it draws its line, and it draws it by aim and not by act: the same getting, guarding, spending, clothing and feeding is not counted as unwholesome when it is done from faith, kindness, compassion or practical wisdom about what is useful [C005-M:L9], and it extends that as far as a valuable garment worn specifically to escape being looked down on [C005-M:L15–L19]. The Pradeepika extract for the same concept carries no life situations at all; it is the bare formal list of the eight greed-rooted minds, and what the list shows is the three conditions that tell them apart — feeling, view and prompting [C005-P:L12] [C005-P:L27–L42]. C006 is where those three conditions are explained one at a time: feeling glad on a pleasant object or flat on a neutral one [C006-P:L25] [C006-P:L74]; a view that denies consequences or excuses the act, with right view found only in wholesome minds [C006-P:L33]; and prompting, which both sources define as including a person's own coaxing of their own hesitating mind [C006-P:L44] [C006-M:L5]. Put on an excavated harbour, the pairing produces the film's whole structure, because this is a place where a system for sorting wanting actually existed, was written down, and survives. A duty was assessed on goods and cargo and a clay seal stamped with a lion certified that it had been paid. That system sorted by act, by weight, by value at the quay. The books sort by three things none of which touches an act. The two sorting systems are laid over each other and do not line up anywhere.
concept_merge.what_it_reveals: That the apparatus which can be excavated and the apparatus the sources describe are not measuring the same thing, and that the film can prove it by withholding. C005 on its own would make a film that audits an ancient trade, which the digest's own limits forbid and which would also be historically ridiculous, since not one of the traders is available to be audited. C006 on its own would make a film about persuasion at a quayside, which there is nothing left to film. Together they set up the only move that works here: the voice performs, out loud, a sorting the camera cannot perform, and the camera performs, out loud, a refusal the voice has already announced. The ranking that flat wanting outweighs glad wanting and that wanting with a justification outweighs wanting without one [C006-M:L19] closes the last escape, because it means that even a complete record of every face at the quay would have sorted nothing. And the absent object finishes the argument. The single cargo anybody can still locate is a fused mound of metal bars on the sea bed that no one who wanted them ever touched. The chain in C005's list runs get, guard, pay out, prepare, use, and this cargo stopped at the second link and has stayed there for two thousand years. A film about wanting whose object is named, located, measured and never seen is not being coy; it is being accurate about what can be evidenced.

concept_links.why: The Margaya's occasions include the whole wealth sequence that a customs post exists to intercept — doing many things to acquire wealth, acquiring it, guarding what has been acquired, paying it out to obtain desirable objects, preparing those objects and consuming them [C005-M:L5] — with the statement that for an ordinary person living apart from the teaching most minds from waking to sleep are of this kind [C005-M:L7], and with seven of the ten unwholesome courses of action carried out through greed-rooted minds [C005-M:L3]. What makes that filmable here rather than accusatory is the rule attached to it: the same acquiring, guarding and spending done from faith, loving-kindness, compassion or practical wisdom about usefulness is explicitly not unwholesome [C005-M:L9], and the source goes as far as allowing a fine or valuable garment worn precisely to escape the contempt of onlookers [C005-M:L15–L19]. Because the line falls on the aim and the outward act is identical either way, the concept can only be demonstrated where an outward act was recorded in enormous detail and the aim was not recorded at all — which is exactly what a stamped customs seal and a two-line rock inscription are. The digest's limits are load-bearing here and are built into the beats rather than left to the risks. The source says nothing against family life and a film must never frame devoted parents as greedy, so nobody in the hamlet at the foot of the rock is framed as a buyer, a seller or a wanter of anything. This is not a case for minimalism or self-denial, since the source allows wealth earned and spent wisely, so the film never moralises about trade, ancient or present. Music, dance and games are in the list because of the enjoying mind and not because the arts are condemned, which is why no beat treats the temple above the site, or anything done in it, as evidence of anything. And the digest records that where the source says an act done from need or wisdom is 'not unwholesome' it does not say what kind of mind it is instead [C005-M:L9], so the film leaves that hole open rather than filling it with a verdict of its own. The Pradeepika's contribution is the bare eightfold list and its three distinguishing conditions [C005-P:L12] [C005-P:L27–L42], which is the structure beat four speaks over a rock face with nothing on it.

C006 is what gives C005's rule moving parts, and it supplies the film's central asymmetry. The sources set the eight minds by three switches: feeling, glad when the object met is pleasant and flat when it is neither pleasant nor unpleasant [C006-P:L25] [C006-P:L74]; a view, meaning in these extracts a denial of consequences or a self-serving excuse, with right view occurring only in wholesome minds [C006-P:L33]; and prompting, which both sources define as including a person urging their own hanging-back mind forward [C006-P:L44] [C006-M:L5]. The Pradeepika's conditions for the sharper, unprompted kind are ordinary and largely external — a sound mind and body, abundant patience, good habit in the task, suitable weather and food [C006-P:L46–L52] — and heaviness belongs only to the prompted side [C006-P:L62]. It also describes, at length and without contempt, the person who believes fully in consequences and still cannot master the craving, mostly through long habit, for gain, or to avoid trouble [C006-P:L66]. None of that leaves physical evidence of any kind, which is precisely why it sits in this film against a harbour whose sorting survives in fired clay. The digest's guards shape what the voice may say. Prompting excuses nothing, so the film offers no alibi to anybody, ancient or present. Calm is not a sign of goodness here, because the Margaya ranks the flat kind stronger [C006-M:L19]; the digest records that this ranking has no commentarial basis in the extract and needs an expert check, so the voice attributes it to the book and does not assert it. The conditions describe tendencies and must not be turned into fate or read as genetics, so they are spoken as conditions beside weather and food and nothing more. And the digest is explicit that wrong view must never be mapped onto any community's faith in a film, so the film names the view switch only in the sources' own terms — denial of consequences, self-serving excuse — and never anywhere near the temple, the monks or the hamlet.

what_the_viewer_could_understand: That the thing which decides what a want is has never left a physical trace, and that this is not mysticism but a plain consequence of a rule the old books state in one sentence: the line falls on the aim, and the outward act is identical on both sides of it. Here that is demonstrable rather than assertable, because a real bureaucracy really did measure, price and stamp the outward act two thousand years ago, and what survives of it is an amount, a harbour, a king and a monastery — and not one word about why anybody wanted anything. The second thing the viewer could take is smaller and harder: that a piece of evidence and a piece of footage are the same kind of object, and that the most honest thing either can do is sometimes to announce what it cannot deliver.
what_must_be_real: The rock, the letters, the light that makes them legible and the light that takes them away. The inscription is filmed as it is, in whatever light actually falls on it; it is never chalked, wetted, powdered, raked with an added lamp or enhanced in the grade to make the letters read, and if the natural light does not give them on the days available, the beat is short or it is cut. **Nothing archaeological is filmed, dived on, approached, lifted, handled, arranged or borrowed.** The wreck specifically is not filmed, not dived, not approached by boat and not represented by any substitute, stock, reconstruction, animation or footage of another wreck; the clay seals, the coins, the glass and the metal are spoken about and never shown, whether they sit in a museum case, a store or a trench, and no excavation in progress is entered. The camera's closest approach to any of it is the ground it came out of. The donation of the customs duty is handled as evidence and never as a virtue: no beat, caption or line of narration attributes merit, piety, generosity or wisdom to a king, and the inscription's own wording is quoted as the wording of a record. The ancient trade is never narrated as a golden age, and the modern deep-water commercial harbour along the coast is not this film's subject; if it is visible it is not framed as a comparison, a contrast, an irony or a comment, and at most it is mentioned as a fact of geography. The temple on the rock is in use. No act of worship is interrupted, restarted, repeated or lit; nobody is asked to be in frame who cannot meaningfully refuse; and no monk or resident is presented as an illustration of anything the narration says. The hamlet at the foot of the rock is a working fishing village, not an inheritance of an ancient port: no fisherman, trader, boat owner or child is framed as a buyer, a seller or a wanter, and nobody in frame illustrates a mental state. The beach is a protected nesting ground; no nesting turtle, track or nest is lit, approached, followed or filmed, and no night work of any kind happens on the sand. The held water shot is a real continuous take on real water at the stated bearing, not a stitched or looped plate.
position_hint: closing candidate for the group: the group's arc ends where wanting meets a wall, and this is the film in which the object of the wanting is named, located, measured and permanently out of reach — the last possible statement of the subject after the earlier films have shown wanting in the presence of its objects. No location reasoning is involved.
risks: The group's specific problem, stated plainly: a camera cannot show greed. The digests say so, and this film's whole method is built on admitting it. A single knowing cut — a face, then an object — would undo the piece.

Showing the wreck, or anything that stands in for it. Any dive footage, any artefact in a case, any reconstruction, any borrowed wreck plate collapses the film, because the withholding is the argument and not a production constraint dressed up as one.

Narrating a king's merit, piety or generosity. The donation of the customs duty is evidence that a harbour existed and that duty was collected there. It is not a virtue and the film does not treat it as one.

Narrating the ancient trade as a golden age, or letting the modern deep-water harbour along the coast into the film as a comparison. That comparison carries political freight the film has no business carrying and is not its subject.
Letting the word greed attach to anybody, ancient or living, in the narration, the captions or the edit. The sources do not licence it of a person and the film never uses it of one.

Framing families or parents as greedy. The digest is explicit that the source says nothing against family life and that devoted parents must not be shown that way, which matters in a hamlet where the film is filming around people's houses.

Drifting into austerity or a lesson about simple living. The source allows wealth earned and spent wisely and a valuable garment worn to escape contempt [C005-M:L15–L19], and the film must not moralise about anybody's spending in any century.

Stating the source's ranking of flat wanting above glad wanting as established fact. The digest records that the extract gives no commentarial basis for it and that it needs an expert check [C006-M:L19], so the voice attributes it to the book.

Letting the conditions for unprompted wanting be heard as destiny or as genetics; the digest rules that reading out, and in the source they sit beside weather, food and being practised at a task [C006-P:L46–L52].

Bringing wrong view anywhere near the temple, the monks or anybody's faith. In these extracts it means denial of consequences and self-serving excuse [C006-P:L33], and the digest forbids mapping it onto any community's religion.
Treating the temple above the excavated site as an exhibit, or filming worship as spectacle. It is a working temple with a resident community and the film's business is downhill of it.

The nesting beach. Lights, night work, tracks and any approach to a nest are all out, and a sanctuary under the Fauna and Flora Protection Ordinance brings its own permission regime and an accompanying officer.

Drone permission over a protected archaeological site and inside a wildlife sanctuary. It may simply be refused, and the film must survive that; the ground fallback is written into the location notes.

The inscription may not be legible on camera at all. Two lines of shallow letters in an exposed rock face, two thousand years weathered, may not give a usable frame in any available light, and beats one, four and seven all depend on it.

Becoming an archaeology documentary about a shipwreck, which is a film that already exists in several versions and is not this one. The excavation is a fact the voice states once and never a subject the film pursues.
drop_if: Access to the inscription cannot be had without enhancing, chalking, wetting or artificially lighting it, or the letters cannot be read in any natural light available on the days of filming.
Permission to film at the site is conditional on filming archaeological material, an excavation in progress, or the wreck.
The temple cannot be filmed around without interrupting, repeating or lighting an act of worship, or without putting residents in frame who have not freely agreed.

The held water shot cannot be obtained as a single continuous take from a position on land or from a static boat outside the sanctuary's seaward limit, in which case the film has no payoff and no substitute for it.
The sanctuary permission required for the beach and the inshore water cannot be obtained, or can only be obtained on terms that put lights or night activity on a nesting beach.

connections.note: That film is the series' sea film and may carry underwater material off a headland at the other end of the island. This one is coastal and deliberately carries none: its object is offshore, named, located, measured and never seen. The two must not be planned as a pair of dive films, and if underwater work is available on this coast it still does not enter this record.

Two coasts and two opposite treatments. That one is full of what the sea gives up, landed and handled in front of the camera; this one is a held frame of water with the object under it, and nothing in the film to touch.
The same two concepts' switches, one where the goods are in your hand at the roadside and one where the goods have been on the sea bed for two thousand years.

selection.reason: A place where the history is the argument: a harbour attested by one sentence cut in rock, a tax on other people's wanting stamped in clay with a lion, and an object of wanting lying offshore that can be named and located and cannot be shown. It breaks the group's monoculture of markets and trades, and its treatment — withholding, long static takes, no goods in frame at all — shares its visual approach with nothing else in the group.

review.note: Replaced entirely. The previous film was a weekly highland fair on a bare rectangle of ground between terraced vegetable hills, and it was one of five films in this group about buying and selling; Chathura's ruling on 25 September 2026 was that all fourteen films here were working places, markets or trades with no historical story between them, and that a group cannot be a monoculture. This record is now bound to a documented history instead of to a resemblance: an ancient port on the maritime route whose existence rests on a single two-line Later Brahmi inscription cut in the face of a coastal rock, recording that the customs duty of the harbour was granted by King Gamani Abhaya to the monastery on the rock above it — the only written evidence that a harbour existed there at all, and described in the literature as the sole surviving evidence, anywhere in this ocean at that period, for the transfer of customs duties to a monastery. Joint German and local excavations from 1994 onwards found the footings of a customs office, a landing jetty on stone pillars, Roman and other foreign coins, and clay seals stamped with a lion that certified that duty on goods and cargo had been paid; offshore lies the oldest wreck known in this ocean, found in 2003 by two local divers, carrying a fused mound of corroded metal bars, several hundred glass ingots, grinding stones and pottery, and still under excavation. The philosophical binding is exact rather than analogical: C005 draws its line by aim and not by act, which means that a bureaucracy which measured, priced and stamped the act recorded everything except the thing the books sort by, and C006's three switches — glad or flat, with a justifying story or without, unprompted or pushed — leave no physical trace of any kind. The film is therefore built as the group's withholding film: long static takes, a river mouth, an inscription that only exists in raking light, no goods in frame anywhere, and a payoff that is a held shot of empty water while the voice states exactly what lies under it and how far offshore. The wreck is never shown, on constraint and on principle — it is under excavation and almost certainly inaccessible, and its absence is the argument. New title, with the old one kept in aliases. Both concept links re-tested against their digests and rewritten; the digests' limits on family, austerity, the arts, wrong view and the conditions-not-destiny reading are carried in the links and the risks. A `connections` entry records that this film deliberately carries no underwater material, so it does not collide with the GRP-01 headland film that may. Body rewritten, so any earlier verdict on the old fair is void and refers to a place this record no longer visits.

suggested_location.region: Hambantota District, Southern Province, on the dry south-east coast between Ambalantota and Hambantota; the rock stands on the bay of Godavaya, with the Walawe river discharging into the sea about four kilometres to the west and the Hambantota deep-water harbour about six kilometres to the east
suggested_location.why_here: Because the history here is the argument and not a resemblance, and because the argument requires an object the film cannot show. This is a place that existed for one reason — other people's wanting, carried across an ocean — and the only sentence about it that survived two thousand years is a tax record: two lines cut into the face of the rock, stating that the customs duty of the harbour was granted by a king to the monastery above it. That inscription is the sole written evidence that a harbour was ever here. Everything else about the port is inference from excavation: pillar stumps of a jetty, the footings of a customs office ornamented with an elephant and lotus flowers, Roman and other foreign coins, and clay seals stamped with a lion that certified duty paid on goods and cargo. Wanting was measured, priced, sealed and handed away, and the seal certified the act and nothing else — which is exactly the distinction C005 draws when it says the line falls on the aim and not on the act. And then the site supplies the one thing no other location on the slate can: the cargo. Four kilometres offshore and thirty-three metres down lies the oldest wreck known in this ocean, carrying a fused mound of corroded metal bars, several hundred glass ingots, grinding stones and pottery, none of which reached anybody who wanted it. It is under long-running excavation and is almost certainly not accessible, and that is not a problem to be worked around: a film about wanting whose object is named, located, measured and never shown is saying the thing a camera cannot otherwise say. Cinematically the place gives a low rock over open ocean, a shallow inscription that exists only in raking light, a wide sand-bar river mouth, an abandoned half-cut pillar lying where it was left, and an empty horizon that can be held for minutes without a single event in it — which is the treatment nothing else in the group is using.

historical_thread.story:
On the dry south-east coast of the island, between the modern towns of Ambalantota and Hambantota, a low granite rock stands over a bay, and the fishing hamlet at its foot is called Godavaya or Godawaya. The name descends from Goda Pavata Pattana or Gota Pabbata Pattana, which means small rock harbour, and it is the rock that gave it. From at least the second century CE the settlement was an entrepôt on the maritime route, lying on the neck of land between an inland harbour on the Walawe river and a sea harbour on the bay, and serving the interior settlements of Tissamaharama and Ridiyagama in the kingdom of Ruhuna. Himanshu Prabha Ray's The Archaeology of Seafaring in Ancient South Asia places it in that network. The Walawe gave easy access upriver to the gem country of the Walawe basin, a source of the dark red garnets that turn up as grave goods across early medieval Europe; ships from the west and ships from China are reported to have exchanged cargoes here rather than going further, and the place remained an important transit port until about the sixth century. In the eleventh century it was the seaport of the southern capital Maha Nagakula on the same river.

All of that is reconstruction. The one piece of writing that establishes a harbour was ever here is cut into the face of the main boulder of the rock. It is two lines long, in Later Brahmi script and Old Sinhala language, in letterforms of the first or second century CE, with letters between about two and a half and six inches high. Senarat Paranavitana read it and published it; his transcript runs 'Siddham [|*] Godapavata-patanahi su[ka]su[ri]yi / raja Gamani Abaya viharata dini', and his translation is 'Success! The customs duties of the port of Godapavata, King Gamani Abhaya granted to the Vihara.' Nothing else says the harbour existed. There is no plan, no ledger, no manifest and no list of goods — only the statement that a duty was collected and where it went. The literature calls it the only concrete evidence confirming the ancient port, and the sole evidence for the transfer of customs duties to a monastery anywhere in the Indian Ocean world at that period. Who Gamani Abhaya was is not settled: probably Gajabahu I, whose reign is variously given as 112–134, 113–135 or 114–136 CE, though an earlier ruler such as Amanda Gamini Abhaya, placed in the 20s or early 30s CE, is also proposed; the Department of Archaeology's own board at the site reportedly takes the Gajabahu identification. On the same boulder is a fragment of a further record of about the sixth century, and a sixth-century inscription names the monastery Godava-vahera. Oliver Kessler published a paper in 1999 on a further, then unknown, second-century inscription of Gajabahu I from the site.

From 1994 a team of German archaeologists from the University of Bonn, directed by Helmut Roth with Udo Recker from 1994 to 1996 and Oliver Kessler from 1997, excavated the site jointly with the Department of Archaeology of Sri Lanka under its Director General W. H. Wijeyapala and with the German Archaeological Institute. Their report on the 1994–1997 seasons appeared in the first volume of Ancient Ruhuna, published at Mainz in 2001. What came out of the ground was the apparatus of a working port: an ancient landing jetty built on stone pillars standing up to three and a half metres high, a large stone anchor found underwater, Roman coins, Han pottery, Sassanian Persian material, beads and bangles, and bricks carrying guild marks in the shape of an O. On the east side they found a building identified as a customs office, decorated with an ornament of an elephant placing its trunk in lotus flowers. And in it they found clay seals bearing the emblem of a lion, which had been used to seal goods and cargo as proof that the customs duty had been paid. On the west side of the monastery they found an elevated image house and a chapter house, a standing Buddha figure about three and a half metres tall and two Bodhisattva figures about one metre eighty each, with traces of a weather-resistant colouring whose source is unclear, indicating a date before the eighth century. A quarry was found as well, with one large pillar covered in drill marks and datable to the middle Anuradhapura period before the fifth century, lying unfinished in front of the huge rock close to the ocean. In August 2008 a human skeleton, with animal-bone and stone tools, was found in an abandoned stone quarry on the site and reported as five to seven thousand years old, with carbon dating not then done; the finds were nicknamed Olli, after Oliver Kessler.

The monastery above is still a working temple. The stupa at the highest point of the rock was renovated around 1920 and the preaching hall and monks' residence were added in the 1930s; ruined pillars, pillar foundations and brick monuments lie around the compound, with a damaged Buddha torso and a moonstone among them. When the tsunami of 26 December 2004 came ashore, the villagers of the hamlet, among them two archaeologists, took refuge in the temple on the rock, and the hamlet recorded no deaths where the surrounding coast lost thousands.

In 2003 two local conch divers working off the hamlet brought up a stone object and took it to the German archaeologists then excavating the port; the Institute of Nautical Archaeology names them as B. G. Preminda and Sunil Ratnaweerapatabandige. What they had found was a wreck, lying about four kilometres offshore at a depth of around thirty-three metres. Systematic diving began in 2008 under the Department of Archaeology and the Maritime Archaeology Unit; archaeologists from the Institute of Nautical Archaeology assessed the site in 2010, and full excavation campaigns began in 2012, with a 2012–2013 season worked by a multinational team of some two dozen archaeologists and students from the United States, France, Sri Lanka and Türkiye. Work paused between about 2014 and 2017 and resumed afterwards. The cargo, as reported, is a concreted mound of corroded iron and copper bars fused into a single lump by time and seawater, together with glass ingots — one account gives more than four hundred, blue-green and black, reported as originating on the Tamil coast of south India — stone querns or bench-like objects, bronze implements, beads and pottery including black-and-red ware. Radiocarbon analysis of the ship's timbers puts it in the last two centuries BCE or the first century CE, and it is described as the oldest known shipwreck in the Asia-Pacific region and probably the oldest in the Indian Ocean. A doctoral dissertation on the metal cargo, An Ancient Iron Cargo in the Indian Ocean: The Godavaya Shipwreck, was submitted at Texas A&M University in 2015. In 2024 a grant of 82,192 US dollars from the U.S. Ambassadors Fund for Cultural Preservation was announced for the Central Cultural Fund's Maritime Archaeology Unit, to document and conserve the wreck and its artefacts over two years; nearly two hundred artefacts have been conserved and the site has been surveyed with three-dimensional modelling.

One more layer of the place has nothing to do with any of this. On 10 May 2006 a 3.85-kilometre section of the beach was declared the Godavaya Sanctuary under the Fauna and Flora Protection Ordinance, extending five hundred metres into the sea and one hundred metres inland from the high-tide line. Five of the world's seven marine turtle species nest here, and it is reported as possibly the best leatherback nesting beach on the island.
historical_thread.how_it_binds:
C005 asks its question by drawing a line, and drawing it in a particular place: not between one act and another, but between one aim and another behind acts that look identical. The same acquiring, guarding and spending of wealth is greed-rooted when it is done for taste, beauty, display or amusement, and is not counted as unwholesome at all when it is done from faith, kindness, compassion or a plain practical sense of what is useful. The consequence is severe and is what makes the concept hard to film: whatever you record of the act, you have recorded nothing about which side of the line it fell on.

This site is the strongest demonstration of that consequence available, because here somebody actually built the machine for recording the act, and it survives. A duty was assessed on goods and cargo at a harbour. A clay seal stamped with a lion was applied as proof that the duty had been paid. The assessment fixed a value, the seal fixed the fact of payment, and a sentence on the rock fixed where the money went. It is a complete audit trail of an outward act, two thousand years old, still readable, and it is silent on every single thing the sources sort by. A camera in the customs office would have added nothing: it would have seen the goods weighed and the clay pressed, which is what we already know. The distinction the concept draws is not hidden by poor evidence here. It is untouched by excellent evidence, which is a different and much stronger point.

C006 supplies the reason it is untouched. The eight greed-rooted minds are distinguished by three things: whether the feeling is glad or flat, whether a justifying story is present or absent, and whether the wanting rose sharply of itself or needed a push — including the push a person gives their own hanging-back mind. None of the three is an act. None of the three has a weight, a value or a customs class. The conditions the Pradeepika gives for the unprompted kind — a sound mind and body, patience, practice in the task, suitable weather and food — are conditions of the person and the day, and the film can speak them over open water without implicating anybody, which is exactly the use the digest's guards permit. The Margaya's ranking sharpens it once more: if flat wanting outweighs glad wanting, then even a complete visual record of every face on the quay would have ranked nothing correctly. The sorting was never available from outside, in the second century or now.

And then the place supplies the object, and withholds it. C005's wealth sequence runs as a chain: do many things to get wealth, get it, guard what is got, pay it out to obtain what is wanted, prepare those things, use them. Four kilometres offshore is a cargo that stopped at the middle of that chain and has stayed there for two millennia — metal bars corroded into one mass, several hundred glass ingots, grinding stones, pottery. Somebody wanted every item of it. Nobody who wanted it received it, wore it, guarded it or used it. It is the physical remainder of wanting with its object subtracted, and it is under excavation and not accessible to a film crew. That constraint and the argument are the same thing. A film about wanting that names its object, gives its bearing, its depth and its contents, and then holds a locked frame on the surface of the water for minutes without showing it, is doing on screen precisely what the sources say about evidence: the outward thing can be measured to any precision you like, and the part that matters is not in it.
what_is_certain: Godavaya or Godawaya is a small fishing hamlet on the coast of the Hambantota District, Southern Province, between Ambalantota and Hambantota. The name derives from Goda Pavata Pattana or Gota Pabbata Pattana, 'small rock harbour', from the rock overlooking the ocean at whose foot it stands. The Walawe river discharges into the sea a few kilometres to the west.

The site has been excavated by German and Sri Lankan archaeologists since 1994: a University of Bonn team directed by Helmut Roth, with Udo Recker (1994–1996) and Oliver Kessler (1997 onwards), jointly with the Department of Archaeology of Sri Lanka under Director General W. H. Wijeyapala and the German Archaeological Institute. The excavation report for 1994–1997 was published as Kessler, Roth, Recker and Wijeypala, 'The Godavaya Harbour Site. Report on the Excavations 1994–1997', in Ancient Ruhuna: Sri Lankan-German Archaeological Project in the Southern Province, vol. 1, Mainz 2001.

The key inscription is cut into the face of the main rock boulder at the site, next to the ancient shrine. It is two lines long, in Later Brahmi script and the Old Sinhala language, with letterforms of the first or second century CE, and letters reported as between about 2.5 and 6 inches high. Paranavitana's transcript is 'Siddham [|*] Godapavata-patanahi su[ka]su[ri]yi / raja Gamani Abaya viharata dini' and his translation is 'Success! The customs duties of the port of Godapavata, King Gamani Abhaya granted to the Vihara.' Citation: Paranavitana, 1983, p. 101.

The literature describes this inscription as the only concrete evidence confirming that an ancient port existed at Godavaya, and as the sole evidence for the transfer of customs duties to a monastery in the Indian Ocean world at that period.
A fragment of a further record of about the sixth century is on the same boulder (Paranavitana, 1983), and a sixth-century inscription names the temple Godava-vahera (Nicholas, 1963).

Oliver Kessler published a paper on excavations at Godavaya together with a then recently unearthed, hitherto unknown second-century inscription of King Gajabahu I, delivered at the fifteenth conference of the European Association of South Asian Archaeologists at Leiden in July 1999 and printed in the proceedings.

Finds from the excavations include Roman coins, Han pottery, Sassanian Persian material, beads and bangles, bricks carrying guild marks in the shape of an 'O', an ancient landing jetty constructed on stone pillars up to 3.50 metres high, and a large ancient stone anchor found underwater.

A customs office building was found, decorated with an ornament showing an elephant placing its trunk in lotus flowers, and clay seals bearing the emblem of a lion were found, which had been used to seal goods and cargo as proof that the customs duty had been paid.

In the monastery area Kessler's team found an elevated image house and a chapter house on the west side, a standing Buddha figure about 3.50 metres tall and two Bodhisattva figures about 1.80 metres each, with traces of a weather-resistant colouring of unclear source indicating a date before the eighth century.

A quarry was found at the site. One large pillar covered in many drill marks, dated to the middle Anuradhapura period before the fifth century, lies unfinished in front of the huge rock, close to the ocean.

The temple on the rock is a working temple. The stupa at the highest point was renovated around 1920, and the preaching hall and the monks' residence were added in the 1930s. Ruins of ancient buildings — pillars, pillar foundations and brick monuments — survive in the temple premises, with a damaged Buddha torso and a moonstone reported among them.

In August 2008 a human skeleton, together with animal-bone and stone tools, was found in an abandoned stone quarry at Godavaya and reported as dating to roughly 3000–5000 BC, with carbon dating not then carried out. The finds were nicknamed 'Olli 1–3' after the German archaeologist Oliver Kessler.

The wreck offshore was found in 2003 by two local divers who brought up a stone object and took it to the German archaeologists then excavating the port; the Institute of Nautical Archaeology names them as B. G. Preminda and Sunil Ratnaweerapatabandige. It lies approximately 4 km offshore at a depth of about 33 metres (reported variously as 32 m, 33 m and 110 feet).

The wreck's reported cargo is a concreted mound of corroded iron and copper bars, glass ingots (one account gives more than four hundred; blue-green and black, reported as originating on the Tamil coast of south India), stone querns or bench-like objects, bronze implements, beads, and pottery including black-and-red ware.
It is widely described as the oldest known shipwreck in the Asia-Pacific region and probably the oldest in the Indian Ocean.

Excavation history as reported: preliminary underwater exploration by the Department of Archaeology and the Maritime Archaeology Unit from 2008; assessment visits by Institute of Nautical Archaeology archaeologists in 2010; full excavation campaigns from 2012, with a 2012–2013 season worked by a multinational team of about two dozen archaeologists and students from the United States, France, Sri Lanka and Türkiye; a pause reported between about 2014 and 2017, with work resuming afterwards and continuing.
A doctoral dissertation on the metal cargo, A. M. Dimucci, 'An Ancient Iron Cargo in the Indian Ocean: The Godavaya Shipwreck', was submitted to Texas A&M University in 2015.

A grant of US$82,192 from the U.S. Ambassadors Fund for Cultural Preservation was announced by Ambassador Julie Chung to Sri Lanka's Central Cultural Fund, at the Maritime Archaeology Museum in Galle Fort, for the documentation and conservation of the Godawaya shipwreck and its artefacts over two years. Nearly two hundred artefacts have been conserved and three-dimensional modelling has been used to survey the site.

A 3.85 km section of the beach at Godavaya was declared the Godavaya Sanctuary under the Fauna and Flora Protection Ordinance on 10 May 2006, extending 500 metres into the sea and 100 metres inland from the high-tide level. Five of the world's seven marine turtle species are recorded there and it is reported as possibly the best leatherback nesting beach on the island.

When the tsunami of 26 December 2004 struck, the villagers of the hamlet, among them two archaeologists, took refuge in the temple on the rock, and the hamlet is reported to have had no fatalities where the surrounding coast lost thousands.
what_is_disputed: Which king the inscription names. 'Gamani Abhaya' is read with confidence; the identification is not. The standard reference literature gives it as probably Gajabahu I, with an earlier ruler such as Amanda Gamini Abhaya, placed in the 20s or early 30s CE, offered as an alternative, and the Department of Archaeology's notice board at the site is reported as supporting the Gajabahu identification. The film does not settle it and does not put a date on the inscription in the voice.
Gajabahu I's regnal dates. Sources consulted give 112–134, 113–135 and 114–136 CE. The film gives none of them.

Who founded the monastery, and when. The reference literature attributes Gothapabbata Vihara to Gotabhaya, ruler of Rohana, early in the second century CE (Abeyawardana, 2004; Nicholas, 1963); one site gazetteer gives the second century BCE and makes Gotabaya the father of Kavantissa; a newspaper account gives the third century BC. Separately, the Mahavamsa's chapter on the twelve kings lists Gotapabbata in the south among seven viharas built by Mahallaka Naga during a six-year reign, after the death of his son-in-law Gajabahu. The chronicle and the inscription therefore cannot both be straightforward accounts of the same founding, and the film records that they disagree rather than reconciling them.

The wreck's date, which is held apart from the inscription's. Reported ranges are: the last two centuries BCE or the first century CE (Institute of Nautical Archaeology); approximately 200–40 BCE from radiocarbon analysis reported in 2012 (Central Cultural Fund National Shipwreck Database); and second century BCE to second century CE (Gaur et al., 2011; Muthucumarana et al., 2014). The wreck is therefore probably one to three centuries older than the inscription, and the two are not evidence of each other. The film does not imply that this ship was carrying the cargo the inscription taxed.

When and by whom the wreck was found. Most accounts give 2003 and two local conch divers or fishermen, with the Maritime Archaeology Unit's first systematic dives in 2008; at least one account dates the discovery itself to 2008 and credits the Maritime Archaeology Unit.

The distance offshore and the depth. Reported as roughly 3 km at about 30 m in one early account, and about 4 km at 32–33 m in later ones. The voice in beat six states four kilometres and thirty-three metres; if a pre-visit establishes different figures, the line changes to match, because the whole point of that beat is that the figures are exact.

Coordinates. Published coordinates for this site vary widely and at least one commonly cited figure (6.00368 N, 80.25766 E) cannot be correct, plotting far to the west of the district. The coordinate recorded here is an OpenStreetMap node named for the temple on the rock; the positions of the inscription, the excavated harbour area, the quarry pillar and the wreck must all be fixed on the ground.

The trade narrative. That ships from the west and ships from China exchanged cargoes here rather than sailing further, that the port remained an important transit point until the sixth century, and that the garnets of early medieval European graves came up the Walawe from the gem basin, all reach this research through secondary and newspaper accounts rather than through excavation reports read directly. The film treats none of it as established and narrates no golden age.

Whether the breakwaters of the modern deep-water commercial harbour a few kilometres east are visible from the rock or from the beach. Not verified. Either way the film does not make a comparison of it.

what_to_film: The inscription, at both ends of the day, on the days the light gives it: locked off, long lens, tight enough that the two lines fill the frame, and held long enough for the shadows to move and the letters to go. This is the film's first and last image and it is filmed as found — no chalk, no water, no powder, no added light, no grade recovery.
The same frame of rock at midday, identical and blank, which is beat four. It only works if it is demonstrably the same piece of stone.
The excavated jetty pillar stumps at low water from the beach and, if the water is clear, from directly above at the surface — the stumps only, never entered, never touched.
The footings of the customs office and the surrounding excavated ground, wide and static in flat light, with nothing in the frame held, moved or pointed at.
The abandoned half-dressed pillar lying near the water, in two shots: one wide enough to show it lying where it was left, and one close enough that the drill marks read as tool marks.
The mouth of the river four kilometres west: the colour join over the sand bar, on a long lens from the beach, at first light and again with the wind up.

The held frame of open water from the top of the rock on the wreck's bearing, locked off, long lens, flat midday light, recorded as one continuous take several minutes long with nothing in it. This is the payoff and everything else is built around obtaining it.
The rock and the temple above it from the beach and from the water, wide, for two or three establishing frames — the temple as a shape on a skyline, never as a subject.
Ambient sound throughout, on its own, long: surf, wind on the rock, the hamlet at a distance, and the flat nothing over the water.
suggested_location.access: By road from the A2 coast highway, turning off between Ambalantota and Hambantota onto a narrow village road that runs down to a sandy compound under large trees at the foot of the rock; roughly 10 km south-east of Ambalantota and around 16–17 km from Hambantota, about twenty to thirty minutes' drive. The temple on the rock is reached on foot up steps from the compound and is a working temple with a resident community, so access to it is the incumbent's to give and is a separate matter from access to the archaeological ground. The excavated harbour area and the rock inscription are on a protected archaeological site: the Department of Archaeology's permission is required for filming and is also the prerequisite for any drone work. The beach and the inshore strip are inside a wildlife sanctuary declared under the Fauna and Flora Protection Ordinance, which brings the Department of Wildlife Conservation into it; its published filming conditions require a wildlife officer to accompany the crew and prohibit sound, flash or artificial light that could disturb wildlife, which on a leatherback nesting beach should be read as ruling out night work altogether. **Drone permission over an archaeological site is uncertain and over a sanctuary may be refused outright.** The published route is a Ministry of Defence security clearance submitted well in advance together with no-objection letters from the relevant site authorities — here the Department of Archaeology and the Department of Wildlife Conservation — followed by an operating approval from the Civil Aviation Authority on form CAA/AS/017 with third-party insurance; special clearance inside a restricted area is described as needing fourteen days' notice. Assume it will not be granted. **The ground fallback is complete and loses nothing:** every shot in the sequence as written is obtainable on foot, because the film's payoff is a locked-off long-lens frame of water from the top of the rock rather than an aerial, the inscription and the pillar are close work, and the jetty stumps and the river mouth are beach positions. The two or three wide establishing frames of the rock can be taken from the beach and, if a boat can be used outside the sanctuary's five-hundred-metre seaward limit, from the water. No boat is needed over the wreck and none is chartered to it. The nearest deep-water commercial harbour is a few kilometres east along the coast, which is worth knowing for logistics and for nothing else.
suggested_location.best_time: The drier, calmer stretch on this coast, broadly the south-west monsoon months from about May to September, when the dry zone here gets least rain and the sea and the sand bar are readable; the north-east monsoon months from about October to January put the weather and the swell on this shore. Within the day, the inscription only in the first or last hour of sun and only on a clear morning or evening — it should be attempted on several separate days rather than gambled on one. The river mouth at first light before the wind. The held water shot at flat high sun, deliberately the worst light of the day, because the frame is about there being nothing in it. The turtle nesting season is a reason to stay off the beach at night, not a reason to visit.

suggested_location.research_note: All of this is desk research by web search on 25 September 2026, and none of it has been checked on the ground or against printed editions. The inscription's transcript, translation, script, language, line count and the Paranavitana citation are as published by lankapradeepa.com, which cites Paranavitana 1983 p. 101 together with Abeyawardana 2004 and Nicholas 1963; the letter heights come from amazinglanka.com. Paranavitana's volume itself was not consulted, and the transcript is reproduced exactly as that secondary source prints it, including its bracketed readings. The excavation history, the personnel, the customs office, the elephant-and-lotus ornament, the lion-stamped clay seals, the jetty pillars, the stone anchor, the guild-marked bricks, the coins and pottery, the statues, the quarry pillar and the 2008 skeleton are from the Wikipedia article on the site, which sources most of them to a 2002 Sunday Times feature and to Kessler's published reports; the reports themselves were not read. The wreck's depth, distance, cargo, dating and excavation seasons are cross-read between the Central Cultural Fund's National Shipwreck Database, the Institute of Nautical Archaeology's project page, Live Science, and the lankapradeepa summary of Gaur et al. 2011 and Muthucumarana et al. 2014, and where they disagree the disagreement is recorded in what_is_disputed and is not resolved. The US Ambassadors Fund grant figure and the conservation numbers come from press coverage; the U.S. Embassy's own pages returned 403 to this research and were not read directly. The Mahavamsa passage on Mahallaka Naga's seven viharas was read in Geiger's translation as published at lakdiva.org.lk, which prints that chapter without verse numbers. **Coordinates: the value written here, 6.1095 N 81.0518 E, is an OpenStreetMap node named 'Gotha Pabbatha Raja Maha Viharaya', cross-checked against a nearby OpenStreetMap viewpoint node named for the sanctuary at 6.1067 N 81.0507 E. It is not a surveyed position for the inscription.** Published coordinates for this site are inconsistent and one commonly cited figure (6.00368 N, 80.25766 E) is impossible. The distance from the rock to the present discharge of the Walawe river was computed from the Wikipedia coordinate for that discharge (6.10528 N, 81.01583 E) and comes out at about four kilometres, so the river-mouth beats and the rock are two separate positions and not one frame; the distance to the modern deep-water harbour's breakwaters, computed the same way, is about six kilometres. Both figures are desk arithmetic on desk coordinates. Access, the state of the village road, whether the inscription is legible in available light, whether the excavated harbour area is exposed or backfilled, whether the quarry pillar is still where it is described, the temple incumbent's willingness, archaeological and wildlife filming permissions, drone permission and the current accessibility of the wreck site are all unverified. **Images: Commons was searched through the search API for the site name in both spellings, for the ancient name, for the temple, for the wreck, for the harbour and for the river mouth, and by category. It holds nothing at all for the rock, the temple, the inscription, the excavated port or the wreck. The only two files it holds for this place are the pair used above, both uploaded by the same contributor and both described as views of this beach in rain, and both were confirmed to exist by action=query&titles= before their URLs were written. No picture of another ancient port, another inscription or another wreck has been substituted, because a photogenic picture of somewhere else would be worse than none.**

unknowns: No permission of any kind has been sought or confirmed. Archaeological filming permission, wildlife sanctuary filming permission, the temple incumbent's consent and any drone clearance are all research directions and nothing more.

Drone permission over a protected archaeological site inside a wildlife sanctuary is uncertain and may be refused outright. The ground fallback in the access notes is written on the assumption that it will be.

Whether the two-line inscription is legible on camera in naturally available raking light has not been established, and three of the seven beats depend on it. It may not give a usable frame at all, and the film accepts that rather than enhancing it.

The wreck's exact bearing from the rock, its distance and its depth need fixing before beat six is written to final, because that beat's whole force is that the figures are precise. Published figures differ.

Whether the excavated harbour features named in the shot list — the jetty pillar stumps, the customs office footings, the unfinished quarry pillar — are currently exposed, backfilled, fenced, overgrown or gone has not been checked. Some of the descriptions relied on here date from the 1990s and early 2000s.

Whether the counterintuitive ranking of flat wanting above glad wanting holds outside this one extract is flagged in the digest as needing an expert check before the film leans on it, which is why the voice attributes it.
evidence_class_note: Editorial proposal. The location is Claude's suggestion and awaits Chathura's verdict; its supporting detail, including the whole historical thread, is desk research by web search and is unverified against printed editions or on the ground. No scene or shot is decided here.
